newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's Lebed under fire in Duma over Chechnya.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Lebed under fire in Duma over Chechnya.

text.p: Russian security chief Alexander Lebed ran into heavy fire on Wednesday in the State Duma lower chamber of parliament over a peace deal with Chechen separatists that deputies said could lead to the country breaking up.

The blunt-speaking Lebed, who ended 21 months of war in the Chechnya region by striking a compromise with rebel leaders, was heckled as he took the podium to defend the agreement he signed on August 31 in the southern town of Khasavyurt.
Lebed rejected accusations that the agreement, which called for Russian troop withdrawals and postponed a decision on Chechnya's status for five years, would violate Russia's territorial integrity.
But some deputies opposed to the deal jeered and shouted "shame, shame" and "traitor".

The fierce abuse came on the eve of a new round of peace talks in Moscow. Chechen separatist leader Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev, due to arrive on Thursday, was sticking by demands for Chechen independence, Interfax news agency said.

After delivering his report and listening to a barrage of criticism from subsequent speakers, including Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov, Lebed attempted to defend his position but eventually left the noisy chamber in frustration.
"Respected deputies, thank you," he snapped before pushing his way to the exit through a mass of journalists and deputies.
In his speech earlier, he dismissed accusations that Russia was quitting Chechnya. "Russia is not leaving Chechnya and should not leave it," he said.
"We have put an end to something that could bring shame (on Russia) for many long years to come," he said, adding that 80,000-100,000 people had been killed in the conflict.
But Kulikov, who has been named by Lebed as one of those responsible for the Chechnya war, described the peace accords as "a cover for most humiliating unilateral concessions".

Viktor Ilyukhin, the communist head of the Duma's security committee, was even more scathing. "The Khasavyurt agreements amount to the complete capitulation of Russia...The ambitions of the separatists are completely satisfied."
Ilyukhin and ultra-nationalist leader Vladimir Zhirinovsky said Lebed might not have understood the implications of his initiative and suggested he might have been set up by his political opponents.
But Lebed, who agreed some people wanted him to fail in his role as President Boris Yeltsin's special envoy to Chechnya, was in combative mood.

"You don't have to pity me. I was a paratroop general and I never pitied anyone when I fought," he said. "I am ready to crush all those political and personal stupidities which have been uttered here today."
He scorned those who demanded that the Chechen opposition be disarmed, the war ended and Russia's integrity preserved.
"And in their opinion this should be done by purely peaceful means," he said sarcastically. "I will not comment on this. You either need a magician, a golden fish or something like this."
He said the Khasavyurt deal had been approved by Yeltsin and Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and was only the start of a long process that would satisfy the interests of both sides.

Kulikov said the Chechens were violating the agreements. "These documents are not only being violated but they are being trampled on in the most rude way at every step," he said in a speech which was greeted with thunderous applause.
"The Chechen separatists are behaving in such a way as if the question of Chechnya seceding has already been decided."
Duma Defence Committee Chairman Lev Rokhlin said Moscow should be under no illusions about the intentions of the separatists. "The rebels were not fighting to stay within Russia," he said.
